analysis.one_liner: Gives federal regulators power over tobacco products, bans most tobacco ads, and penalizes makers if teen smoking doesn't fall.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to regulate tobacco and cut teen smoking got a hearing and two committee working sessions in early 1998 but was never sent to the full Senate, and it died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The PAST Act would have set national targets to cut daily tobacco use among people under 18 by 60% within ten years, with financial surcharges on cigarette makers if the targets were missed. It would have given the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to regulate tobacco like other risky products — requiring ingredient disclosure, manufacturing standards, and stark rotating health warnings covering a quarter of the package front. It would have banned outdoor, Internet, cartoon, and sponsorship advertising, restricted how tobacco is sold, funded state prevention and quitting programs from a Tobacco Settlement Trust Fund, and directed a new federal standard limiting secondhand smoke in workplaces.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teens, who the bill targets as virtually all new tobacco users, by cutting off the advertising and access that recruit them. Adult smokers who want to quit, through federally funded state cessation programs. Nonsmokers, through a new indoor-air standard limiting secondhand smoke at work. All paid for by the tobacco industry through fees and penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Sets national goals to cut daily tobacco use among minors by 30% in years five and six, 50% in years seven through nine, and 60% thereafter, and imposes surcharges on manufacturers if the targets are missed.

Requires manufacturers to disclose all ingredients and nicotine content and submit health-risk assessments, and authorizes standards that could gradually reduce nicotine yields, ban harmful additives, and reduce cigarette-induced fires.

Replaces small printed Surgeon General notices with nine blunt rotating warnings — 'Cigarettes Are Addictive,' 'Smoking Can Kill You' — covering at least 25% of the front of every pack and 20% of every print ad, printed in alternating black-on-white and white-on-black.

Bans outdoor advertising including billboards and stadiums, cartoon characters like the ones used to sell cigarettes, Internet advertising, payments to place products in movies and video games, and brand-name event sponsorship, and restricts most other ads to black text on white.

Bars sale of tobacco to anyone under 18, requires photo ID for buyers under 27 and face-to-face transactions, bans free samples and vending machines except in adults-only facilities, and sets up a state licensing system with random unannounced compliance checks using minors.

Sends $65 million a year to states for retailer licensing plus allotted funds for state and community prevention programs and smoking-cessation treatment, all drawn from a Tobacco Settlement Trust Fund funded by the industry, and directs a federal workplace indoor-air standard on tobacco smoke within 12 months.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who would pay $100 million in annual regulatory fees, face surcharges if youth use doesn't fall fast enough, and lose most ways to advertise. Retailers and distributors, who would need licenses, run ID checks, and face civil and criminal penalties. Adult smokers would likely pay more per pack as industry costs were passed through — which is partly the point, since higher prices deter teen smoking.

drawbacks.text: The bill treats tobacco as a product that stays on the market: it bars the Secretary from banning a class of tobacco products or eliminating nicotine without Congress passing an approving joint resolution, gives the tobacco industry seats on the waiver board that reviews exemption petitions, and shields tobacco growers from any added regulatory burden beyond other farm commodities.

It creates a 'reduced risk tobacco product' pathway letting manufacturers market products as less harmful based on short-term testing, with the patent holder able to charge competitors fees to license the technology — a framework that could let companies sell 'safer' cigarettes with limited long-term evidence.

The compliance load lands partly on small retailers, who would need state licenses within 30 days, face random inspections with underage test buyers, and bear penalties — including $250 a day for selling without a license — for their own or their employees' violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits — fewer kids addicted to nicotine, honest warnings, funded quitting programs, cleaner workplace air — are large and well documented in the bill's own findings, which call tobacco the nation's number one preventable cause of death. The real costs fall on the industry being regulated and on retailers absorbing paperwork; higher prices for adult smokers are a cost but also the main lever for cutting youth use. The design is imperfect — it entrenches growers, seats industry on its waiver board, and opens a 'reduced risk' marketing lane — but on balance the trade is heavily favorable to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee that received the bill held a hearing and two working sessions in February and March 1998 but never reported it to the full Senate, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeffords introduced the PAST Act on February 12, 1998, joined by three Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which held a hearing on February 24, 1998.
The committee held consideration and markup sessions on March 11 and March 18, 1998 — the stage where a committee rewrites and votes a bill out — but no further action was ever taken on the bill.
The bill's last recorded action was the March 18, 1998 markup; the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill, and no House companion action appears in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they went on selling and marketing cigarettes for years with none of the bill's federal product regulation, advertising bans, or youth-use surcharges. Congress did not give the FDA authority over tobacco until 2009, a decade later. Smokers and would-be young smokers got none of the prevention and cessation programs the bill would have funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco manufacturers, unregulated for another decade

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PAST Act and, as a member of the committee handling it, saw it through a hearing and two markup sessions before it stalled.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Conducted a widely reported national advertising and lobbying campaign against the 1998 tobacco-control legislative effort in Congress; no activity by the industry on S. 1648 itself appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican senator with three Republican cosponsors and referred to a committee that worked on it, so its sponsorship was bipartisan-leaning; because it never reached a floor vote, no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected cigarette and smokeless tobacco makers to FDA-style oversight: ingredient and nicotine disclosure, manufacturing standards, $100 million in annual fees, surcharges if youth use targets were missed, and near-total loss of advertising channels. Every restriction it imposed was designed to shrink the number of new customers the industry recruits from children.

The bill bars any regulation that would burden tobacco farmers more than other commodity producers, protecting the agricultural supply chain even as it regulated manufacturers. Their livelihood depends on continued tobacco consumption, which conflicts with the bill's public-health goals.

Bans on billboards, stadium and event sponsorship, cartoons, and Internet ads — plus black-text-on-white format rules — would have eliminated most tobacco advertising revenue for media outlets and promotion firms. That revenue came from marketing a product the bill's findings call inherently unsafe.

Retailers would need state licenses, run photo-ID checks, end self-service and vending sales, and face civil and criminal penalties and random inspections — real compliance costs. Their interest in unrestricted sales, including to minors who buy most of their own cigarettes, runs against the bill's purpose.
